summary: Gives basic recommendations for running a country-level X.500 Directory Service Agent as part of a production directory service. It is informational guidance rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1803 gives advice on running a country's part of a shared X.500 directory as a real service rather than an experiment. It sets targets for uptime, for how fast the operators must answer mail, and for what each organisation running a server must provide.

subtitle: Basic service targets for running a country-level X.500 directory server as a production service rather than a pilot.

tldr.problem: Parts of the global X.500 directory were still run as pilot projects, with poor availability and inconsistent information quality, partly because there were no formal service objectives.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out recommendations for the country-level master DSA and its shadows, for the organisation that runs the service, for the people who staff it, for DSAs in the national directory and for the software they run.
tldr.outcome: It calls these recommendations only a starting point toward a production-quality X.500 infrastructure, and says it does not discuss the move from the 1988 X.500 standard to the 1993 one. The memo is Informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 1803 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text calls its recommendations a starting point rather than a standard, and says it does not discuss the move from the 1988 X.500 standard to the 1993 one.

sections.title: Why a Production Directory Is Needed
sections.content:
The ISO/CCITT X.500 Directory standard enables the creation of a single world-wide Directory holding information about various types of information, including people. In the United States, NYSERNet started a White-pages Pilot Project in mid 1989, and the project was later taken over by Performance Systems International. Several organisations in the United States joined it, and the PSI project provided the c=US root level master Directory System Agent, a DSA, where the organisations that joined the pilot were connected. In November 1990 the PARADISE project started in Europe to provide an international directory service across Europe with international connectivity to the rest of the world, and it operated the root of the world DSA that connected each of the national pilots into a single world-wide Directory Information Tree, enabling information about people all over the world to be obtained using an Internet Directory User Agent.

The memo says much of the criticism of X.500 stems from the lack of a production quality infrastructure. Although there were already well over 500 organisations and 1,000,000 entries in the X.500 directory, some portions were still considered a pilot project. Poor availability of parts of the directory and inconsistent quality of information are two problems that had not been adequately addressed in a number of the pilot projects, one reason being a lack of formal service objectives for running an X.500 service, and recommendations for achieving them.

It makes one point about where quality is decided: the country-level DSAs form the access path for the rest of the world to reach the directory entries of that country's organisations, so the availability and performance of the country-level DSAs give an upper bound on the quality of service of the whole country's part of the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared directory worked, but some parts were slow, sometimes offline or out of date. Since everyone reaches a country's listings through that country's own servers, those servers set the limit on how good the whole country's part can be.

sections.title: Running the Country-Level Master DSA
sections.content:
The recommendations are split into operational recommendations for the organisation running the master DSA, DSA recommendations, and personnel recommendations. On operations, the country-level data should be available for querying 100 percent of the time, and availability for updating is also important but may be slightly reduced in practice, given X.500's single master scheme.

The master DSA should be available at least 95 percent of the time, which means it must be monitored and supported over the weekend. The master DSA and its shadows should be positioned to minimise the possibility of single points of failure, and should be spread across the national network infrastructure to distribute the load and bring information closer to requesters. Country DIT information, including naming infrastructure such as localities and states, should be replicated across the oceans, not only to serve when the trans-oceanic links go down but also to handle name resolution for clients in other countries; the memo suggests a complete copy of the US root in Europe and a copy of the Japanese root in Africa and North America, and says generally data should be replicated wherever it is heavily used and wherever it will be needed during a network partition. The master and shadow DSAs must run software that conforms to the recommendations in section 4.

For the service provider, the memo recommends providing a generic e-mail address for the DSA manager, with more than one manager available so the manager can go on vacation, and answering mail to the manager promptly. All mail should be acknowledged as received within one working day. Trouble reports about the master and shadow DSAs must be answered within 24 hours, with a resolution where possible; there are situations where problem resolution may take longer than 24 hours, but this should be unusual. General informational requests, such as how to join the service and where to get the software, should be acknowledged within 2 working days and normally resolved within 2 working days.

The provider should keep a current e-mail distribution list of all DSA managers within the country, with changes made within 2 working days, and it may be useful to include X.500 software vendors and funders on the list. Changes and additions to the national master DSA, such as requests to add an organisation, to change a DSA's information or to remove a DSA, should get a quick turn around of 2 working days, with acknowledgements within 1 working day. The manager should make available documentation about the X.500 Production Service, covering how to join, which software to run and where to obtain it, naming guidelines, schema requirements and operational requirements, and should ideally advertise the service and solicit new members. If the service is operating at pilot level, references to pilot should be removed and a transition process established with the national-level DSA managers, including a new set of requirements for their DSAs in the production service.

Organisations and their DSAs that do not meet the published operational guidelines should be removed, with DSA managers notified at least 4 weeks in advance so they can correct their deficiencies, the procedure performed at least once every 3 months, and a grace period of 3 months given to new organisations. The service provider should also work with other national X.500 service providers in the same country to ensure a single consistent DIT within the country; in North America the production service should act as an ADDMD in the North American Directory Forum service, producing timely Knowledge and Naming updates for the Central Administration when entries under c=US or c=CA change, and applying the updates produced by other ADDMDs, so that there is a single consistent DIT common to both.

For personnel, the memo asks the country-level master DSA to take part in technical forums, to provide a help desk for DSA managers facing operational problems, with support by e-mail and optionally by telephone, above and beyond what the mailing list gives. It should publish quarterly status reports giving details on the state of the service, such as new and deleted organisations, statistics on the availability of the master and shadow DSAs, and the number of operations performed. It should also provide electronic access to service information, for example a World Wide Web page describing the service with contact information, pointers to useful software and a form for comments and bug reports, plus FTP access to the same information.
sections.plainLanguage: The main copy of the directory should almost always be open, spare copies should be kept in different places, and the people who run the service should answer mail quickly and publish reports on how it is doing.

sections.title: Rules for Running a DSA
sections.content:
These recommendations apply to all DSAs operating within the country-level Directory Management Domain. The availability of the organisation's subtree should be as close to 100 percent as possible, and that coverage shall be provided by a master DSA and zero or more shadow DSAs.

Organisations should maintain information in their DSAs that is complete, accurate and up to date, and that information shall be accessible through Directory protocols to the extent allowed by the security and privacy policies of the respective organisations.

Organisations still experimenting with the Directory should either be marked clearly as experimental, for example with an appropriate Quality of Service attribute, or perhaps by including the word experimental as part of the organisation's RDN, or they should be listed in a separate portion of the namespace, also clearly marked. Once the organisation is done experimenting it can move to the production part of the DIT. Two contact persons must be named as DSA managers for each DSA, and the DSA software should conform to the recommendations in section 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who runs a piece of the directory must keep it correct and online, name two people to call, and label test entries so that nobody mistakes them for real ones.

sections.title: Rules for DSA Software
sections.content: The software should support the attributes and object classes found in the Internet schema, which is specified in RFC 1274. It should be reliable, supportable and should provide sufficient performance to handle the DSA traffic. Additional requirements may be imposed by the service provider, for example '93 replication.
sections.plainLanguage: The server software has to speak the agreed set of fields and kinds of entry, be dependable, be one the operators can support, and be quick enough for the traffic it carries.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Open Work
sections.content:
The memo states only that security issues are not discussed in it.

The abstract sets out the limits of the advice. The recommendations can only be considered a starting point in the quest to create a global production quality X.500 infrastructure, and for there to be a true production quality infrastructure more work must be done, including a transition from the 1988 X.500, plus some Internet extensions, to the 1993 X.500 standard, including the '93 replication and knowledge model. The memo does not discuss this transition.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not cover safety, and it says this is a first set of rules with more work to do.

viz.caption: THE SERVICE TARGETS THE MEMEO SETS

items.title: Master DSA uptime
items.text: At least 95 percent, monitored and supported over the weekend.

items.title: Query availability
items.text: Country-level data should be queryable 100 percent of the time.

items.title: Mail to the manager
items.text: Acknowledged as received within one working day.

items.title: Trouble reports
items.text: Answered within 24 hours, with a resolution where possible.

items.title: General questions
items.text: Acknowledged within 2 working days and normally resolved within 2 working days.

items.title: Changes to the master DSA
items.text: Turned around in 2 working days, acknowledged within 1 working day.

items.title: Removing an organisation
items.text: At least 4 weeks of notice, and the procedure run at least once every 3 months.

items.title: New organisations
items.text: A grace period of 3 months to come up to speed.
